nameStory: The Green Aeolis gets its name from its lovely green coloration, which helps it blend in perfectly with the green algae and seaweeds it calls home. The word 'aeolis' comes from ancient Greek, referring to the finger-like projections called cerata that cover its back like tiny green flames dancing in the current.
description: The Green Aeolis is a tiny sea slug, one of the nudibranch family, that looks like a miniature underwater dragon. These soft-bodied marine creatures typically measure less than an inch long and sport dozens of finger-like projections called cerata covering their backs. Their vibrant green color and translucent body make them living jewels of New England's rocky shores. Unlike snails, they have no shell and breathe through those colorful projections on their backs.

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Bright to deep green body color that can appear almost emerald in good light, often with translucent quality that lets you see internal structures

idTips.label: Finger-like cerata
idTips.description: Dozens of slender, finger-like projections covering the back that feel soft and squishy to gentle touch, often with colorful tips

idTips.label: Two pairs of tentacles
idTips.description: Four horn-like tentacles on the head - two rhinophores that smell the water and two oral tentacles near the mouth

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Semi-transparent body wall that reveals internal organs as darker shadows, giving it a glass-like appearance

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically under one inch long, about the size of your thumbnail, with a soft gelatinous texture throughout

habitat: Look for Green Aeolis in shallow rocky tide pools and on rocky substrates along New England's coast, especially where green algae and hydroids are abundant. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found clinging to the undersides of rocks or nestled among seaweed at low tide. You'll have the best luck finding them in the lower intertidal zone where they can stay moist between tides.

seasonality.spring: Active and feeding as water temperatures rise, often found grazing on early season algae growth in tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation when they're most active and numerous, easily spotted during low tide exploration.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but less active as temperatures cool, may be found in deeper pools that retain warmth longer.
seasonality.winter: Difficult to find as they retreat to deeper waters or become inactive, rarely seen in accessible tide pools.

funFact: Green Aeolis can steal the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and store them in the tips of their finger-like projections, essentially turning their prey's weapons into their own personal defense system - like a tiny underwater Robin Hood!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small green anemones or other green nudibranchs, but the Green Aeolis moves in a distinctive gliding motion and has those characteristic finger-like projections that wave gently in the current. Remember: if it's crawling smoothly and has dozens of green 'fingers,' you've found your aeolis!
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name has recently changed from Diaphoreolis viridis to Tenellia viridis due to genetic studies that rearranged nudibranch classification, so you might see it listed under either name in older field guides. This is common with sea slugs as scientists continue to untangle their complex evolutionary relationships.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives the Naked Ear Aeolid which lacks the vibrant green color, or the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid which has distinctive spots, the Green Aeolis maintains its solid green coloration throughout its body and cerata. The other Tenellia species in New England tend to be more orange, brown, or spotted, making the Green Aeolis the easiest to identify by color alone.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tenellia relatives, the Naked Ear Aeolid is distinguished by its particularly translucent appearance and the arrangement of its cerata.
Unlike its relative the Green Aeolis which has a more uniform greenish coloration, the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid displays distinct dark spots on a translucent background.
Unlike the Green Aeolis which has a distinctly greenish coloration, Tenellia pustulata is more translucent with its characteristic bumpy texture.
Compared to the Green Aeolis (Tenellia viridis), this species shows more orange or golden coloration rather than green tones.
